accuracy_findings.claim: Moons and asteroids never get a share either. Housing built there still counts for the whole system.
accuracy_findings.problem: No building in the game can give housing on a moon or asteroid, so 'Housing built there' describes something that cannot happen. Moons and asteroids use orbital buildings, and no orbital building gives housing at any speed. The page's own table 'Buildings that give housing' lists only Habitable Planet and Sterile Planet buildings, so the sentence contradicts it and suggests a player can build housing in orbit. The first half is true: compute_local_population only walks the top-level bodies (stellar_system.ex:1449-1476), so moons and asteroids always get 0.
accuracy_findings.evidence: tmp/help-review/housing-acc-r0-biomes.exs (RC.Help.Data.buildings(:slow)): the buildings with sys_habitation output are infra_open (open), infra_dome (dome), hab_open (open), hab_dome (dome), hab_open_poor (open) and hab_open_rich (open). The orbital-biome buildings (mine_orbital, factory_orbital, research_orbital, finance_orbital, spatioport_orbital, defense_local_orbital, happy_pot_orbital, happy_orbital, shipyard_1..4_orbital, radar_orbital) have no sys_habitation output. stellar-body.ex gives moon and asteroid the biome :orbital. The grep of lib/ finds sys_habitation outputs only in building-*.ex plus a mutator (mutators are excluded from the tables).
accuracy_findings.fix: Drop the second sentence. Keep 'Moons and asteroids never get a share.' followed by the existing 'Buildings on moons and asteroids still mobilize workforce.' If a reason helps, say no building on a moon or asteroid gives housing.

accuracy_findings.claim: Example with 23 workforce: planet with 13 housing from buildings: 19 population / planet with 3 housing from buildings: 4 population
accuracy_findings.problem: The numbers are correct, but the scenario is unusual. 23 workforce against 16 total housing means population sits well above its growth target (16.75) and is shrinking. The rounding (19 and 4 from exact shares 18.69 and 4.31) also pulls the reader's attention without being explained.
accuracy_findings.evidence: tmp/help-review/housing-acc-r0-apportion.exs: StellarSystem.apportion_workforce(23, [13, 3]) => [19, 4]; apportion_workforce(23, [13, 0, 3]) => [19, 0, 4] (a gas giant or asteroid belt in between gets 0); apportion_workforce(15, [10, 0]) => [15, 0] (matches the screenshot, a Megapolis planet and a barren planet with no housing).
accuracy_findings.fix: Optional. Use a workforce at or below housing, for example 16 workforce split 13 and 3, where the exact shares are whole numbers and no rounding is involved (16*13/16 = 13, 16*3/16 = 3). Or keep the current numbers, which are correct.

clarity_findings.fix: Drop the caption (or shorten the lead-in sentence) so the shot's one allowed caption carries the only restatement, per rule 8's "at most one caption sentence."

clarity_findings.claim: "The shares are counted again only when the workforce changes by a whole point" is harder to parse than it needs to be.
clarity_findings.problem: "Counted again" is vague about what recomputes; a player has to infer this is about recalculation timing, which is a minor stumble for a page otherwise written in very plain language.
clarity_findings.fix: Reword to something like "A planet's share is recalculated only when the system's workforce changes by a whole point."

accuracy_findings.claim: Example with 16 workforce: planet with 13 housing from buildings: 13 population / planet with 3 housing from buildings: 3 population
accuracy_findings.problem: The numbers are right, but workforce (16) equals total building housing (13 + 3), so each planet's share comes out equal to its housing. A player can read this as 'a planet's population equals its housing', not 'a share in proportion to housing'. The earlier 23-workforce example (19 and 4) showed the proportion better. The screenshot shows the same effect: 15 population on a planet whose Megapolis gives 10 housing.
accuracy_findings.fix: Pick a workforce different from the total housing so the split is clearly proportional, e.g. 8 workforce with the same planets gives [7, 1]. Run apportion_workforce to confirm before writing it. Or add one line: the shares always add up to the system's workforce, not to its housing.

clarity_findings.claim: "Each planet gets a share in proportion to the housing its own buildings give." reads awkwardly for a phrase meant to be a simple, friendly sentence (style rule 1).
clarity_findings.problem: "the housing its own buildings give" is a clunky noun-clause construction a player has to re-read once to parse; it slows an otherwise clean paragraph.
clarity_findings.fix: Reword to something like "Each planet's share matches how much housing its own buildings give."

clarity_findings.claim: "A planet's share is recalculated only when the system's workforce changes by a whole point." is stated with no consequence attached.
clarity_findings.problem: This is an implementation-cadence detail. A reader sees it and has no way to tell why it matters (does a number sometimes look stale? is there a delay after colonizing a new planet?), so it reads as trivia rather than something actionable.
clarity_findings.fix: Either drop the sentence (it is not called out in the guide map's owns list for housing) or add the one consequence a player would notice, e.g. "so a planet's number can lag a tick behind a workforce change."

clarity_findings.claim: "Gas giants and asteroid belts have no tiles, so they never get a share." and "Moons and asteroids never get a share either. No building there gives housing." are three short sentences all making the same "gets no share" point about different body types.
clarity_findings.problem: Splitting one idea (which bodies get none) across two bullets and three sentences is slightly more fragmented than necessary for a 180-word leaf; a reader has to hold the same conclusion twice.
clarity_findings.fix: Combine into one bullet, e.g. "Gas giants, asteroid belts, moons and asteroids never get a share. None of them can build housing."
